item.title: Mukta bodha intro
item.description: Emerging sometime in the middle of the sixth century, the Śivadharmaśāstra represents a non-Brāhmaṇa tradition of dharmaśāstra that provides the foundation for many common features defining Śaiva identity. It is the text that introduces Sanskrit literature to the narrative of the manifestation of liṅgodbhavamūrti, to the centrality of the mantra Oṃ namaḥ Śivāya to Śaiva tradition, and that for the first time equates the regularized installation and collective veneration of the Śivaliṅga with the defining features of the now-familiar Śaiva social and institutional worlds it vividly imagines into being. The Śivadharmaśāstra proclaims that its very essence (sāra) is Śivabhakti. As taught here directly by Śiva himself, bhakti involves a multidimensional eightfold practice of 1) tenderness towards Śiva’s devotees, 2) delight in watching others perform pūjā, 3) one’s own worship, 4) arcanā with bhakti for one’s own sake and bodily effort for the sake of devotion, 5) bhakti when listening to Śiva’s stories, 6) spontaneous transformations of the limbs and eyes and the production of sounds as a consequence of bhakti, 7) constant recollection of Śiva, and 8) a livelihood dependent upon Śiva. In contrast to the difficult, expensive, and restrictive rituals of the Veda, bhakti as taught by the Śivadharmaśāstra is represented as an easeful means (sukhopāya) accessible to all human beings regardless of social status, that bestows both spiritual and concrete material benefit, facilitates self-deification in a manner that has real-life consequences, and ultimately makes possible freedom from saṃsāra. As understood by its many centuries of interpreters, this Śivadharma serves either to mitigate or entirely nullify matters of varṇa and jāti, substituting in their place a fervent commitment to upholding Śaiva norms.
